Case 01 · USA · Health

Parents use a chatbot to focus the search

Two scientist parents used a chatbot to work through their daughter's lab results, then took the leads to the specialists who made the diagnosis.

At a glance

The problem
A 5‑year‑old with developmental delays, poor wound healing, low antibodies and infections most days of the year.
AI used
ChatGPT, a general‑purpose chatbot.
What goes in
Lab results and symptoms, with the question “With the following test results, what are possible diagnoses?”
What comes out
Possible diagnoses, and later the genes linked to her connective‑tissue and immune problems.
Who checks it
Specialists at Boston Children's Hospital, including Dr. Wendy Chung, who co‑discovered the syndrome.
Diagnosis
Okur‑Chung neurodevelopmental syndrome, about 1 in 100,000 people.

Step by step

  1. Person

    Hilary and Matt Eaton gather Olivia's lab results and describe her symptoms.

  2. AI

    The chatbot first suggests common variable immunodeficiency. That's wrong, but it points them at her immune system.

  3. Person

    They keep asking, and use it to list genes linked to her connective‑tissue and immune problems.

  4. Expert

    Boston Children's specialists confirm the syndrome and start monthly antibody infusions and anti‑seizure medication.

  5. Outcome

    She sleeps through the night, has far fewer infections, and has missed only three days of school.

Why it worked

The parents used AI to ask better questions and arrived at specialists with focused leads.

Limits

Its first answer was wrong, and the family had expertise most parents don't.

Build a similar prototype

Real tools you can use to build a learning prototype of this kind of service. A prototype is for learning only: anything touching health needs clinical validation and regulatory approval.

Models
Claude, GPT‑4o or Gemini (hosted), or Llama and Mistral run locally with Ollama
Medical knowledge
Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) for symptoms, ClinVar and OMIM for genes
Genetics tools
Exomiser or LIRICAL, open‑source tools that rank genetic variants against symptoms
Interface
Streamlit or Gradio for a simple upload‑and‑ask web app

Case 02 · USA · Disability

A wireless implant that speaks for her

A fully implanted device reads individual neurons and sends their activity wirelessly to software that speaks her words aloud.

At a glance

The problem
Progressive motor neuron disease was taking away her speech.
AI used
Decoding software that learns to map patterns of neural activity onto words.
What goes in
Signals from 421 micro‑wires in the motor cortex, sent wirelessly from a fully implanted device.
What comes out
On‑screen text and synthesized speech in real time.
Who checks it
The Connect‑One early feasibility study at University of Michigan Health, approved by the FDA in November 2025.
Status
One participant, early company‑reported results, not yet peer reviewed.

Step by step

  1. Expert

    June 2026: surgeons at University of Michigan Health implant the device in a four‑hour operation.

  2. Person

    She tries to speak, either moving her mouth or only imagining the words.

  3. AI

    The implant records individual neurons and transmits the activity wirelessly to an external computer.

  4. AI

    Decoding software turns the patterns into words, shows them as text and speaks them in a synthesized voice.

  5. Outcome

    Her first free sentence, “Okay, I have a lot to say,” was decoded without errors. She has phoned her grandchildren with it.

Why it worked

Because the device is fully implanted and wireless, nothing passes through the skin, which suits everyday home use.

Limits

One person, results reported by the company, and long‑term safety and accuracy are unknown. A six‑year follow‑up is planned.

Build a similar prototype

Real tools you can use to build a learning prototype of this kind of service. A prototype is for learning only: anything touching health needs clinical validation and regulatory approval.

Practice data
Public intracortical speech datasets released by the BrainGate team (Brain‑to‑Text benchmarks)
Decoding
PyTorch recurrent networks with CTC decoding (torchaudio or pyctcdecode)
Streaming
Lab Streaming Layer (LSL) to simulate a live wireless signal
Voice
Piper or Coqui XTTS for text‑to‑speech

Case 03 · India · Work

A voice assistant that knows each cow

Dairy farmers ask in Gujarati by voice, and the assistant answers using the co‑operative's records for their own animals.

At a glance

The problem
A vet visit costs ₹150 and has to be arranged through the co‑operative.
AI used
Sarlaben, the dairy co‑operative's voice assistant, and MahaVISTAAR, Maharashtra's farm advisory platform.
What goes in
A spoken question in Gujarati or Marathi, the farmer's phone number, and the animal's name or ID.
What comes out
Personal advice on animal health, feeding, breeding, vaccination and government schemes.
Who checks it
Specialists step in for serious cases. The assistant connected Meenaben to one.
Language
Local languages, by voice, so farmers don't need to read or type.

Step by step

  1. Person

    Gayatriben's buffalo keeps banging its head against a tree, so she asks Sarlaben by voice.

  2. AI

    The assistant recognises her phone number and looks up her animals in the co‑op's cattle records.

  3. AI

    It suggests cleaning the area with oil and applying turmeric. The problem clears up.

  4. Expert

    When Meenaben's cow has a difficult birth, the assistant recognises how serious it is and connects her to a specialist.

  5. Outcome

    Meenaben's cow survives. In Maharashtra, Dipali Kalbhor's fertiliser use falls by about 15%.

Why it worked

Linking the assistant to records farmers already have makes the advice specific to their animal, not generic.

Limits

These are farmers' accounts. There is no published evaluation yet, and serious cases still need a vet.

Build a similar prototype

Real tools you can use to build a learning prototype of this kind of service, mostly free or open source.

Phone line
WhatsApp Business Cloud API, or Twilio and Exotel for voice calls
Indian languages
AI4Bharat speech and translation models (IndicConformer, IndicTrans2) or the government's Bhashini APIs
Answers
An LLM with retrieval over veterinary and extension guides, using LlamaIndex and Chroma
Farmer records
PostgreSQL, looked up by caller phone number

Case 04 · USA · Health

An early‑warning alert for sepsis

A model watches each emergency patient's data and alerts a nurse when it sees the early pattern of sepsis.

At a glance

The problem
Sepsis can become deadly within hours, and its early signs are easy to miss in a busy emergency department.
AI used
COMPOSER, a deep‑learning model developed at UC San Diego Health.
What goes in
More than 150 measurements: vital signs, lab results, medications and medical history.
What comes out
An alert sent to the patient's nurse.
Who checks it
A nurse reviews the patient, and a doctor decides what care is needed.
How we know
A before‑and‑after study of 6,217 adults with sepsis, published in npj Digital Medicine.

Step by step

  1. Person

    A patient arrives at one of two UC San Diego Health emergency departments.

  2. AI

    The model keeps checking more than 150 measurements from the patient's record.

  3. AI

    When the pattern suggests sepsis, it sends an alert to the nurse.

  4. Expert

    The nurse examines the patient and raises it with a doctor, who decides on treatment, usually antibiotics given sooner.

  5. Outcome

    Sepsis deaths fell by 17% in relative terms, or 1.9 percentage points, and recommended care was followed more often.

Why it worked

The alert goes to the nurse who is already with the patient, so it fits the existing routine instead of adding a new step.

Limits

A before‑and‑after study in one health system can't prove the AI caused the drop. Wider testing is needed.

Build a similar prototype

Real tools you can use to build a learning prototype of this kind of service. A prototype is for learning only: anything touching health needs clinical validation and regulatory approval.

Practice data
MIMIC‑IV and the PhysioNet/CinC 2019 sepsis challenge data (credentialed access)
Models
XGBoost or LightGBM for tabular risk scores; PyTorch for time‑series models
Hospital data
HAPI FHIR to simulate a hospital record feed
Alerts
A small dashboard in Streamlit or Grafana with nurse acknowledgement

Case 05 · El Salvador · Learning

AI tutors inside a whole‑school reform

AI tutors were one part of a national programme that also improved teaching, coaching and school facilities.

At a glance

The problem
Raising learning across a whole public school system, not just in one classroom.
AI used
AI tutors provided through a government partnership with xAI, announced in December 2025.
What goes in
Students' questions and practice work in class.
What comes out
Tutoring and practice for each student, alongside the teacher's lessons.
Who checks it
Teachers, who also received coaching as part of the programme.
How we know
Results for 1,198 volunteer students in 171 pilot schools, announced by the government and the World Bank.

Step by step

  1. Expert

    The government brings in structured teaching, teacher coaching, catch‑up programmes, management tools and better facilities.

  2. Person

    For just over a year, students in 171 pilot schools use AI tutors as part of their classes.

  3. AI

    The tutors give each student practice and explanations at their own pace.

  4. Expert

    Coached teachers decide what each student needs next.

  5. Outcome

    Tested students scored above national averages in reading, maths and science, comparable to Germany and Sweden on PISA 2022.

Why it worked

The AI came with better teaching, coaching and facilities, not in place of them.

Limits

The schools volunteered, detailed scores aren't published, and the AI's share of the gain can't be separated out.

Build a similar prototype

Real tools you can use to build a learning prototype of this kind of service, mostly free or open source.

Tutor
Open WebUI with Ollama on a school server, with a Socratic system prompt
Curriculum
Retrieval over the national syllabus and open textbooks with LlamaIndex
Low connectivity
Kolibri (Learning Equality) for offline lessons and practice
Teacher view
Moodle or a simple dashboard showing each student's progress

Case 06 · Senegal · Work

Satellite crop maps for small farms

An open‑source model turns a year of satellite images into crop maps detailed enough to show small family plots.

At a glance

The problem
Small plots are hard to map, and ground surveys are slow and expensive.
AI used
Tessera, an open‑source model from University of Cambridge researchers.
What goes in
A full year of satellite images of the region.
What comes out
Crop maps at 10‑metre detail.
Who checks it
Researchers calibrate the model with a small amount of ground data.
Accuracy
84% in Senegal's groundnut basin, up to 28% better than the next best method.

Step by step

  1. AI

    The model reads a full year of satellite images and turns each 10‑metre square into numbers that describe its seasonal changes.

  2. Expert

    Researchers supply a small set of fields where the crop is known on the ground.

  3. AI

    A simple algorithm uses those examples to label crops across the whole region.

  4. Expert

    Governments and food‑security groups can plan with the maps instead of doing costly ground surveys.

  5. Outcome

    Crops mapped with 84% accuracy, using a fraction of the computing power of other methods.

Why it worked

Doing the heavy computation once, in an open model, makes it cheap for anyone to map a new region.

Limits

The benefit to farmers is indirect, through better data for decision makers. Effects on the farms themselves aren't measured yet.

Build a similar prototype

Real tools you can use to build a learning prototype of this kind of service, mostly free or open source.

Model
Tessera itself is open source
Satellite data
Sentinel‑1 and Sentinel‑2 from the Copernicus Data Space, or Google Earth Engine
Libraries
rasterio, xarray and TorchGeo; scikit‑learn for the final classifier
Maps
QGIS to view and share the crop maps
